claims.claim: Political geography is the study of how political power and organization are expressed across space, i.e., how humans divide the Earth's surface for purposes of management and control and what follows from where the lines fall.

A territory is a bounded portion of space over which an authority claims control; territoriality is the strategy of claiming an area and setting the rules for who may enter it and what may happen inside it, and it operates at many scales.
Sovereignty is supreme authority within a territory: a sovereign state has total control over its internal and foreign affairs and is recognized as such by other states.

The Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States (signed 26 December 1933), Article 1, lists four qualifications a state should possess: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states.

The modern idea that the world is partitioned into sovereign states, each supreme within its own territory, is commonly traced to the Peace/Treaty of Westphalia in 1648, which helped establish recognition of the sovereignty of territory ruled by representative government structures in Central Europe.

Political authority is organized across scales; within a state, authority ranges from unitary (concentrated centrally) to federal (constitutionally divided between central and regional governments), and devolution is the transfer of powers from a central government to regional or local governments while the state remains a single sovereign whole (e.g., the UK devolving powers to Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland).

States sometimes pool authority in supranational organizations. The United Nations had 193 member states as of the admission of South Sudan on 14 July 2011 (the count since then). The European Union comprises 27 member states, most sharing the euro as a common currency and permitting passport-free movement across many internal borders, while each remains a sovereign state.

Boundaries divide continuous space into discrete political units; a boundary marks where one state's sovereignty ends and another's begins, defining the territory a government controls and the population it counts, and boundaries are human decisions redrawn over time (e.g., fifteen states emerged from the former Soviet Union in 1991).
Political geography is one of the main subfields of human geography, applying the spatial perspective to the spatial dimension of political processes.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many sovereign states exist, and whether the count equals UN membership.
positions: The UN has 193 member states (since South Sudan's admission on 14 July 2011).

Some entities are widely recognized as sovereign yet are not UN voting members (e.g., Vatican City/Holy See is a permanent observer), so counts of 'sovereign states' can differ from UN membership, and some boundaries and sovereignty claims are disputed.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson cites the UN figure of 193 member states with its date and attribution, notes that recognition and disputed claims make a single 'number of countries' contestable, and avoids asserting a definitive total or taking a side on any specific dispute.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the Peace of Westphalia (1648) truly originated state sovereignty.
positions: It is conventionally credited as the origin of the modern sovereign-state system ('Westphalian sovereignty').
Historians debate how sharp the break was and caution against overstating 1648 as a single origin point.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents Westphalia as the conventional shorthand for the principle of territorial sovereignty and explicitly notes that historians debate how sharp the break was, avoiding overstatement.

Supports: political geography as the study of how humans divide the Earth's surface for management and control; territoriality as establishing rules over a space at multiple scales; the definition of a state and of a sovereign state (total control over internal and foreign affairs plus recognition); territory as a location claimed by a sovereign state; the UN 193-member figure (stated for 2023 on the page); devolution as the breakup/transfer illustrated by the UK; the Treaty of Westphalia (1648) and the sovereignty of territory ruled by representative structures; unitary vs federal arrangement; supranational organizations including the UN and the EU (27 members, common euro currency, passport-free internal movement); boundaries as defining state territory and citizens; and the breakup of the USSR into fifteen states in 1991. sourceRecords.title: Convention on the Rights and Duties of States (Montevideo Convention), Article 1
sourceRecords.provider: Yale Law School, Lillian Goldman Law Library (Avalon Project)
sourceRecords.notes: Primary treaty text (public domain). Signed at Montevideo, Uruguay, 26 December 1933. Article 1: 'The state as a person of international law should possess the following qualifications: a) a permanent population; b) a defined territory; c) government; and d) capacity to enter into relations with the other states.' Used as the source for the four widely cited criteria for statehood; the short Article-1 clause is attributed as a legal fact.

sourceRecords.title: Growth in United Nations Membership
sourceRecords.notes: United Nations. Supports the dated membership figure: the UN grew from 51 original members (1945) to 193 members, reaching 193 with the admission of South Sudan in 2011 (South Sudan admitted 14 July 2011, confirmed via UN News story 381552 and cross-checked against the UN 'Member States' A-Z list, which enumerates 193). Used to date and attribute the 193 figure. No wording reproduced beyond the attributed count and date.
